clinicalPearls: An uncommon, indolent, slowly progressive infection caused by anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria—primarily Actinomyces species—that normally colonize the mouth, colon, and vagina; it has been called one of the most frequently misdiagnosed diseases (Harrison 22e p.1363).

Three classic presentations should trigger suspicion: a chronic mass-like lesion that crosses tissue planes and mimics malignancy, a sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs, and a refractory or relapsing infection after a short course of therapy (Harrison 22e p.1363).

Most infections are polymicrobial; companion organisms such as Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Eikenella corrodens, Enterobacteriaceae, Fusobacterium, and Bacteroides are commonly co-isolated, though their pathogenic contribution is uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1363).

Disease spreads contiguously, ignoring tissue planes; the characteristic chronic phase produces single or multiple indurated lesions with fibrotic walls classically described as wooden (Harrison 22e p.1364).
Central necrosis containing neutrophils and sulfur granules is virtually diagnostic; over time, sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone develop (Harrison 22e p.1364).
Lymphatic spread with lymphadenopathy and distant hematogenous seeding are uncommon—an important contrast with malignancy and tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1364).
Oral–cervicofacial disease is the most frequent presentation, typically at the angle of the jaw, often precipitated by dental disease or procedures (Harrison 22e p.1364).

Pelvic actinomycosis is strongly associated with intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUDs) and other foreign bodies such as surgical mesh; risk increases the longer the device remains in place and is low when in place under one year (Harrison 22e p.1364-1365).

Sulfur granules represent an in vivo matrix of bacteria, calcium phosphate, and host material; on hematoxylin-eosin staining they may be surrounded by a radiating fringe of eosinophilic clubs (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Foreign bodies (especially IUDs) and immunocompromising states—HIV, transplantation, common variable immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, and certain immunosuppressive therapies—are recognized predisposing factors (Harrison 22e p.1364).
FDG-PET may show hypermetabolism in actinomycotic lesions, potentially compounding confusion with malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1365).
harrison.pathophysiology: The etiologic agents are members of the normal oral, gastrointestinal, and female genital flora. The critical initiating step is disruption of the mucosal barrier, allowing local infection. Once established, the infection spreads contiguously in a slow, progressive fashion that disregards normal tissue planes. Although acute inflammation may occur initially, the hallmark is a chronic indolent phase with indurated lesions, central necrosis (neutrophils plus sulfur granules), and dense fibrotic walls. Sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone may develop over time. Foreign bodies, particularly IUDs, facilitate infection, and ulcerative mucosal infections (e.g., HSV, CMV) may promote disease (Harrison 22e p.1364).
additionalDifferentials: Malignancy / solid tumor (most common misdiagnosis given mass-like, tissue-plane-crossing behavior)
Inflammatory bowel disease (when abdominal sinus tracts/fistulas develop)
Bacterial pneumonia or lung neoplasm (in thoracic disease)
infectionMimics: Mycetoma due to Nocardia or Actinomadura species
Botryomycosis (chronic suppurative bacterial infection forming granule-like clumps)
additionalInvestigations: Microscopic identification of sulfur granules in pus or tissue (most common diagnostic means; yield improves with additional histopathologic sections and positively charged slides)
Anaerobic culture—isolation maximized under anaerobic conditions, typically requiring 5–7 days and potentially up to 2–4 weeks; even a single antibiotic dose can preclude recovery
16S rRNA gene amplification and sequencing to enhance sensitivity and specificity
MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (databases still being optimized)
Histologic stains: periodic acid–Schiff (PAS), Grocott methenamine silver (GMS), and Gram stains to identify actinomycotic aggregates
CT and MRI for lesion characterization and monitoring; FDG-PET may demonstrate hypermetabolism
CT/ultrasound-guided aspiration or biopsy to obtain material in a minimally invasive fashion; endometrial biopsy for pelvic disease
redFlags: Chronic mass-like lesion crossing tissue planes and mimicking cancer
Sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs
Refractory or relapsing infection after a short antibiotic course
Lesions crossing fissures/pleura, extending into mediastinum, bone, or chest wall (empyema necessitatis)
Wound or fistula that fails to heal, or recurrent abdominal disease
CNS involvement (brain abscess, meningitis, cavernous sinus syndrome)—a critical-site presentation
harrison.prognosis: Actinomycosis is usually curable with medical therapy alone, even in extensive disease, and an awareness of its clinical spectrum can expedite diagnosis and minimize unnecessary surgery, morbidity, and mortality. Cure of established disease requires prolonged treatment, and relapse is a clinical hallmark if therapy is stopped too early; refractory disease has been described in HIV-infected individuals (Harrison 22e p.1363, p.1366).
pitfalls: Diagnosis is rarely considered prospectively—actinomycosis is often first identified by the pathologist after extensive (and avoidable) surgery (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Prior antibiotic exposure or failure to obtain appropriate anaerobic cultures frequently precludes microbiologic identification; even a single antibiotic dose can prevent isolation (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Because actinomycetes are normal oral and genital-tract flora, their detection in sputum, bronchial washings, or cervicovaginal secretions without sulfur granules may reflect colonization rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.1365).

Detection of Actinomyces-like organisms on Papanicolaou smear in IUD users has low positive predictive value; in an asymptomatic patient this warrants education and follow-up, not routine IUD removal (Harrison 22e p.1365).
Isolation of Actinomyces from blood cultures without a defined focus may represent contamination or transient bacteremia from a mucosal site (Harrison 22e p.1366).
Elevated CA-125 in pelvic disease and FDG-PET hypermetabolism can reinforce a mistaken cancer diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1365).
management: Prolonged penicillin therapy as the mainstay, typically high-dose intravenous benzylpenicillin followed by an extended oral course of penicillin or amoxicillin
Tetracyclines such as doxycycline, macrolides or clindamycin as alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients
Extended treatment duration with clinical and radiological monitoring to secure cure and prevent relapse
Surgical drainage of abscesses, excision of sinus tracts and debridement of extensive or necrotic disease alongside antimicrobials
Removal of predisposing foreign bodies, notably intrauterine contraceptive devices in pelvic disease
Serial CT or MRI, with FDG-PET where used, to monitor treatment response and guide duration
Recognition that companion organisms rarely alter management, as penicillin generally remains effective in polymicrobial disease
